articles.title: HC judge vacancies at decade-low 26%, but pendency keeps piling up
articles.summary: With 64 lakh cases, backlog refuses to ease NEW DELHI: After hovering between 36% and 40% over the past decade, vacancies in HC judges have shown a
articles.body: With 64 lakh cases, backlog refuses to easeNEW DELHI: After hovering between 36% and 40% over the past decade, vacancies in HC judges have shown a significant decline, falling to 26%, this despite sanctioned strength of judges in HCs increasing from 906 in 2014 to 1,122.The largest HC, Allahabad, has brought down its vacancies to 56 against a sanctioned strength of 160 judges, as of Nov 1.The other HCs with bigger benches and usually large vacancies - Bombay, Punjab and Haryana, Madras, Calcutta, Karnataka and Delhi - too, have increased their working strength, bringing down vacancies.The last time judges' vacancies were this low (at 26%) was in July 2009, when there were 234 judges posts to be filled against a sanctioned strength of 886 in 21 HCs then.Vacancies in HCs started gradually climbing thereafter, which coincided with the friction between higher judiciary and govt over an attempt to bring a judicial accountability bill and passage of National Judicial Appointments Commission Act by Parliament. NJAC Act was later struck down by Supreme Court.In Nov 2014, vacancies were at 36% (in 24 HCs), with 353 judges posts vacant against a sanctioned strength of 984. These vacancies remained at 35% in March 2022 with 387 posts vacant, though the sanctioned strength was increased to 1,104 judges.Large vacancies are a prime factor behind backlog of cases. Though SC historically never had large vacancies, case pendency in SC has increased from 52,000 in 2009 to more than 92,000 at present.The situation is worse in HCs and much worse in district and lower judiciary, deteriorating every month. In 2009, total pendency of cases in HCs was at 39.5 lakh, which climbed to 45 lakh in 2013, and is at 64 lakh at present.The pendency in lower judiciary is similarly getting worse while the large number of vacancies remain static at around 5,000 against a sanctioned strength of 25,894 judicial officers.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Kevin Bacon and his brother opened a music room inside the Philadelphia juvenile detention centre where young people can learn music in their mother's memory
articles.summary: A juvenile detention centre in Philadelphia has gained a new space where young people can write songs, learn about music production and record their own
articles.body: A juvenile detention centre in Philadelphia has gained a new space where young people can write songs, learn about music production and record their own work. The studio, named Ruth’s Room after the mother of actors Kevin Bacon and his brother Michael, was officially opened in January 2025 at the Philadelphia Juvenile Justice Services Center, as reported by City of Philadelphia. The project brings together the brothers, local music organisations and community supporters, with the aim of giving detained young people access to creative activities that are often difficult to accommodate within the facility. The room also reflects the family's effort to honour Ruth Bacon's legacy through education and opportunities for young people.Kevin and Michael Bacon support music room named after their motherThe new studio was developed in partnership with Rock to the Future, a Philadelphia-based organisation that provides music education to young people. Kevin and Michael Bacon were among the contributors who helped make the project possible, alongside the organisation SixDegrees.org, The McLean Contributionship, His & Her Interiors and local artist Wendy Medley. Rapper Meek Mill also supported the initiative.The room carries the name of Ruth Bacon, whose work as a justice and education advocate is recognised through the project. Its opening brought together people from the entertainment industry, the local arts community and organisations working with young people in the city's juvenile justice system.Rather than being limited to occasional music activities, the facility has been designed as a dedicated place for lessons, recording and performances.Rock to the Future expands its programme at Philadelphia detention centreRock to the Future began providing music programmes at the Philadelphia Juvenile Justice Services Center in March 2022. Its initial classes reached just 12 young people. Within a little over a year, the programme had expanded considerably, reaching more than 200 young people annually by June 2023. Before the dedicated studio was established, music sessions took place within the centre's residential units. These areas had limited room for activities, while restrictions on access to wider programming could make it difficult to provide consistent opportunities for creative work.The organisation began looking for a suitable space that could accommodate a broader range of activities. The resulting studio was developed to serve as a central location where young people could attend classes, produce music and share their work with others.Jessica Craft, Rock to the Future's chief executive and founder, said, “The young people at the Juvenile Justice Services Center are incredibly talented and motivated.”“It’s an honor and a necessity to provide these youth with opportunities, hope, and a second chance—to ensure their entire humanity is recognized in a world quick to label them.”What young people can do inside Ruth’s RoomThe studio has been designed to accommodate different levels of musical experience. Young people who have never taken part in music lessons can explore an unfamiliar activity, while those who already have an interest in music can work on developing their skills and original material.Its facilities include a recording booth, dedicated areas for music production and a performance stage. Weekly lessons will give residents opportunities to create music, work with other participants and perform their compositions. Families will also be able to attend performances, allowing young people to share what they have been working on during their time at the centre.The programme is not solely focused on producing finished recordings. Group music activities also require participants to listen to one another, communicate ideas and work towards a shared result. The sessions are intended to help develop concentration, discipline, teamwork and a sense of responsibility.The role of music in emotional healing and rehabilitationLife inside a juvenile detention facility can leave young residents with limited opportunities to express themselves. Difficult experiences and emotions may be hard to communicate, particularly in an environment where much of the daily routine is structured around supervision and rehabilitation.Ruth’s Room provides a setting where participants can put some of those feelings into creative work. Writing lyrics, producing recordings and collaborating on songs offer different ways to communicate experiences without necessarily having to explain them directly.The Philadelphia Department of Human Services has also pointed to the potential benefits of music-based activities for young people dealing with challenging circumstances. Music therapy and creative programmes can offer ways to manage stress, improve mood and provide a constructive focus.Kimberly Ali, commissioner of the Department of Human Services, described the studio as an opportunity to give young residents practical skills alongside a greater sense of belonging. The project, she said, extends beyond music-making to the wider experience of learning and developing within a supportive environment.A longer-term role for creative programmes in youth rehabilitationThe opening of Ruth’s Room adds a dedicated facility to a music programme that had already grown considerably since its introduction in 2022. Its recording and performance facilities also give Rock to the Future more scope to work with young residents than was possible when classes were held in their living units.The involvement of families in performances is another part of the programme. It creates opportunities for residents to present their work to people outside the centre and gives relatives a chance to see the skills and interests they are developing.You use AI every day. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Sikkim HC, with a sanctioned strength of three judges but a working strength of two, is unable to hear intra-court appeals against judgements rendered by two single-judge benches headed by the chief justice and the other judge.Pendency of appeals against single-judge bench's orders has forced Sikkim CJ A Muhammed Mustaque to write to CJI Surya Kant for issuance of appropriate orders "for facilitating transfer of five pending writ appeals to another high court or making such other suitable arrangement in the interest of justice".A bench of CJI Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana Friday treated the Sikkim CJ's letter on the administrative side as a suo motu writ petition and sought response from the Centre.Sikkim CJ, in his letter, said, "The continued pendency of these matters, owing to the aforesaid institutional constraint, may adversely affect the timely dispensation of justice and legitimate expectations of the litigants. The situation, therefore, calls for appropriate consideration so that the appeals may be heard and adjudicated upon without undue delay."Justice Mustaque became CJ of Sikkim HC on Jan 4. In June, the HC's first woman judge Meenakshi M Rai became CJ of Patna HC, reducing Sikkim's working strength to two, the other judge in the HC being Justice Bhaskar Raj Pradhan.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Prince William once broke up with Princess Catherine in 2007; royal photographer reveals he wanted to be sure their marriage would last forever, recalls what William told him after their 2010 engagement
articles.summary: Prince William once ended his relationship with Kate Middleton, now Princess Catherine, after nearly five years of dating, but the brief separation in
articles.body: Prince William once ended his relationship with Kate Middleton, now Princess Catherine, after nearly five years of dating, but the brief separation in 2007 reportedly had a specific reason: he wanted to be certain before committing to marriage. Royal photographer Arthur Edwards has now shed light on the future king's explanation, revealing what William told him after announcing his engagement to Catherine in 2010.In an interview on Hello!'s A Right Royal Podcast, Edwards recalled asking William directly why he had broken up with Catherine. According to the photographer, the Prince of Wales said he wanted to be sure that their marriage would last forever.Prince William wanted to be sure before marrying Princess Catherine"When they got engaged, there was a couple of us invited in to meet Catherine," Edwards recalled. "I asked him, 'What did you break up for?' He said, 'Because I wanted to be sure. Because I want this marriage to last forever.'"Edwards suggested that William's experience of his parents' troubled marriage had influenced his approach to relationships."And I think it will," the photographer said of the couple's marriage, adding that William had learned from his parents' broken marriage.William and Catherine first met as students at the University of St. Andrews in 2001. Their friendship eventually developed into a relationship, and they began dating before moving in together. However, after around five years together, they briefly separated in 2007.Royal biographer Robert Jobson described the breakup as an "emotionally-charged 30-minute conversation" over the phone. In his 2024 biography Catherine, The Princess of Wales, he wrote that the split was devastating for Catherine, who felt particularly hurt by being told over the phone. The couple reportedly acknowledged at the time that they were on "different pages".Princess Catherine and Prince William addressed their breakupDuring their engagement interview with ITV's Tom Bradby on November 16, 2010, William and Catherine spoke openly about their brief separation.William said they were both young and still discovering themselves when they decided to take time apart."We were both very young, it was at university, we were both finding ourselves as such and being different characters and stuff, it was very much trying to find our own way, and we were growing up," he explained.He added that the time apart gave them some space and ultimately worked out for the better.Catherine, meanwhile, admitted that she had not been happy about the breakup initially, but felt the experience made her stronger and helped her understand herself better.Royal photographer recalls spotting the couple together after their splitEdwards also recalled an incident at Sandringham when he photographed a group of William's university friends, without realising that Catherine was among them."I was standing around the back where William was out there with some mates from university," he said, explaining that he only recognised Catherine in the photograph years later.He added that she was not someone people would have immediately identified as the woman who would one day become Princess of Wales.The photographer also recalled noticing the couple together at the Concert for Diana in the summer of 2007, just months after their separation. His wife, Ann, spotted Catherine sitting with William in the Royal Box and suggested that the relationship was back on."She said, 'I think it's back on, you know.' And it was," Edwards recalled.William and Catherine announced their engagement in November 2010 and married at Westminster Abbey in April 2011. They marked 15 years of marriage in April 2026.Arthur Edwards praises William and Catherine as a teamReflecting on the couple's journey, Edwards said he believed they had grown into a strong team and praised the way William had handled life in the public eye.He also spoke about William's efforts to protect his children from the media attention he experienced growing up, saying that the Prince of Wales had ensured that his children would not face the same level of intrusion.Edwards described William as having grown into a statesman and praised both him and Catherine for their roles as ambassadors for the country. He also expressed confidence in William's future as king.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A California teenager sends student volunteers into strangers' backyards to pick unwanted fruit; his initiative has now rescued over 11,000 pounds of fruits for people in need
articles.summary: A California teenager has found an unusual way to tackle food waste and hunger by sending student volunteers into strangers' backyards to harvest fruit
articles.body: A California teenager has found an unusual way to tackle food waste and hunger by sending student volunteers into strangers' backyards to harvest fruit that would otherwise go unpicked. Apollo Wong, founder of Glean On Me, started the initiative after noticing fruit rotting on neighbourhood trees while people at a local homeless shelter struggled to access fresh food. He began connecting homeowners with surplus fruit to charities that could distribute it to people in need. What started as a small community effort has grown into a student-led operation involving hundreds of volunteers across Pasadena and the San Gabriel Valley. By August 2026, the initiative reported recovering more than 11,000 pounds of fruit through organised harvesting events.How a teenager came up with the idea of rescuing backyard fruitWong's interest in fruit harvesting began during family gatherings at his Taiwanese grandparents' home. His grandparents had a farm in Taiwan, and picking fruit from their backyard was a regular part of family celebrations, including birthdays and Lunar New Year.The idea for Glean On Me emerged later, when Wong was volunteering at a homeless shelter as part of his school's community service requirements. He noticed the demand for fresh, nutritious food among people experiencing food insecurity. At the same time, he regularly saw fruit falling from trees in neighbourhood gardens because homeowners could not consume or harvest everything their trees produced.He realised that the two problems could be connected. Instead of allowing the surplus fruit to go to waste, it could be collected and delivered to organisations serving people who needed fresh produce.Wong founded Glean On Me in 2024 to put that idea into action. The name combines the word 'glean', which means collecting what would otherwise be left behind, with a reference to Bill Withers' song 'Lean on Me'.How Glean On Me harvests fruit from strangers' backyardsThe initiative works by connecting homeowners who have excess fruit with volunteers and charities that can put the produce to use. Residents can register their properties with the organisation, allowing Wong to coordinate harvesting events when their trees are ready.He recruits mainly middle school and high school students, along with their families, to participate. Before each event, the team coordinates with the property owner and the charity that will receive the harvested fruit.During the harvests, volunteers pick ripe fruit from trees, collect it in containers and prepare it for distribution. Wong also guides younger participants, explaining where the produce will go and why recovering food matters for both the environment and people facing food insecurity.The initiative has turned an ordinary neighbourhood activity into a community effort. Homeowners get help collecting fruit they cannot use themselves, students gain hands-on volunteering experience, and local charities receive fresh produce for their beneficiaries.More than 11,000 pounds of fruit rescued through the initiativeGlean On Me has expanded considerably since its early harvesting events. According to the organisation's reported figures, it had recovered more than 11,000 pounds of fruit by August 2026.The initiative's latest reported impact includes more than 250 volunteers, 24 harvesting events and partnerships with 14 organisations. Its website also reports that the recovered produce has helped nourish more than 6,100 people.Earlier figures show how quickly the project grew. In the summer of 2025, Wong and his volunteers collected more than 5,700 pounds of fruit through 11 harvesting events. That effort involved over 100 student volunteers from 16 schools and supported eight local charities.The project has also expanded beyond individual residential gardens. Volunteers have participated in harvesting activities at locations including the Huntington Library and the Los Angeles County Arboretum, helping recover produce from additional properties.Where the harvested fruit goesThe fruit collected by Glean On Me is distributed through local charities, food banks and organisations that support people experiencing food insecurity.Among the organisations named in the project's earlier reports are Union Station, Friends In Deed and Ronald McDonald House Charities. These organisations serve people and families facing difficult circumstances, including homelessness and financial hardship.The initiative has also worked with Food Forward, a nonprofit that recovers surplus produce and distributes it to hunger-relief organisations. Such partnerships allow the volunteers to connect their harvests with established food-distribution networks rather than having to organise individual deliveries to every recipient.The aim is to move the harvested fruit quickly from the trees to the organisations that can distribute it. This helps ensure that produce collected during the events reaches people while it is still fresh.How the project also helps reduce food wasteGlean On Me addresses an environmental problem alongside food insecurity. Fruit left unpicked eventually falls to the ground and decomposes, even when it is still suitable for consumption.By collecting surplus produce before it goes to waste, the initiative gives homeowners' excess fruit another purpose. Wong has also highlighted the environmental consequences of discarded organic matter, including the methane emissions associated with decomposing food in landfills.The organisation estimates that its work has prevented more than 40,000 pounds of carbon dioxide-equivalent emissions. This is an estimate reported by the initiative, alongside its figures for fruit recovered and people reached.For Wong, the project connects several parts of the community. Homeowners contribute their surplus produce, students give their time, and charities ensure the food reaches people who need it.Recognition and the future of Glean On MeWong's work has received recognition from several organisations. In 2025, Glean On Me was among the top five finalists in the Dragon Kim Foundation's Dragon Challenge, which selected the project from approximately 600 applicant teams. The foundation also provided a $5,000 grant and leadership support to help develop the initiative.In October 2026, Wong was named a Daily Point of Light honoree for his volunteer work. He was also listed among the runners-up for the 2026 Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes, which recognises young people making a positive difference in their communities and the environment.Now a high school senior, Wong is thinking about how the initiative can continue when he leaves for college. He hopes to pass its leadership to another person in the community while remaining involved in its summer activities.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Franz Ferdinand turning to art at Glasgow Print Studio
articles.summary: Kirsty Wark and Sanjeev Kohli are also among those taking part in the Call and Response project.
articles.body:
It was the neighbourhood that launched Franz Ferdinand's career and even got a mention in one of their earliest songs.

"Well here we are at the Transmission party. I love your friends they're all so arty," is the line in their single Do You Want To.

Twenty-one years later, the band are back in the Glasgow Print Studio - two doors down from Transmission Gallery - to launch a limited edition print that celebrates their musical journey and their Scottish roots.

Bassist Bob Hardy said: "When I was a student and we were getting the band together, it was often the openings that would take place on King Street which would be the beginning of a night out.

"Transmission Gallery, the Modern Institute round the corner. It would often be the start of some of the best nights out ever."

The band shot to fame with their 2004 debut, which produced three hit singles in a row and won them the Mercury Prize the following year.

They've since toured the world, notching up a substantial fan base in South America where they did an early tour in support of U2, and playing their own headline residency at the historic Olympia Music Hall in Paris earlier this year.

And it's an image from that landmark show which they chose to make into a work of art as part of Glasgow Print Studio's Call and Response project.

"It's often used in music where you sort of sing the first part and then people respond," said the studio's director Claire Forsyth.

"So seeing what the response is from the participants has been really interesting because it's not always what you might expect."

Among those who've signed up to this "gym for artists" are broadcaster Kirsty Wark, actor Sanjeev Kohli, and musician Bobby Bluebell.

Each worked with master printmakers to create a new work for a limited edition run.

Kirsty Wark was inspired by her great aunt, a bank teller by day, who painted china and porcelain in her evenings. Her delicate print is based on a plate that her aunt painted.

Sanjeev Kohli's work was also personal, and a tribute to his late father. St Parduman of Glasgow shows his father as St Mungo on a gable end, with the words I Belong to Glasgow in English, Gaelic and Punjabi.

Forsyth said: "He was thinking a lot about very traditional Glaswegian elements but then putting a bit of a twist on it.

"'I belong to Glasgow' was something that his dad said after a day or two of being in Glasgow. He said 'I may not always understand what everyone's saying to me but I feel I belong here'. It's a very powerful message."

For all of Franz Ferdinand this was a personal project. But especially for Bob Hardy, who graduated from Glasgow School of Art in 2003 with a degree in painting and printmaking.

"I hadn't done any printmaking since I was 19," he said.

"So it was really nice to be back here and in the workshops. It felt like being back at art school again."

The band had been on tour for two years when the idea was first mooted.

Hardy added: "We had this idea that we wanted to bring the touring world of Franz Ferdinand back to Glasgow.

"Knowing that it was going to be launched after we'd come home.

"We've had this set for the last two years designed by our lighting engineer, Dan Williams, which we've had all over the world and we just wanted to document it."

French photographer Julien Courbe – who was in Glasgow for the launch – captured the original image of the band onstage, which he then developed as a cyanotype in his Paris kitchen. That was then made into a print by Master Printer Alistair Gow.

Thursday's launch was a relatively intimate experience for a band used to playing huge stadiums.

The limited run of a hundred prints was swiftly dispatched, some online to international fans, with the profits going to future workshops for less starry would-be artists.

Forsyth added: "Our aim is for everybody to be able to enjoy it whether it's in our free to access galleries where they do a class or where they join as a member and come use our specialist equipment upstairs.

"You don't need to be an artist to be a printmaker that's what's so great and egalitarian about it."

Alan Cumming, Greg Hemphill and Julie Wilson Nimmo will launch work in coming months while the aptly-named Glasgow band The Pastels will be next to create a work.

It has been a new experience for Franz Ferdinand but one that Bob Hardy, at least, plans to repeat, having been invited back for a printmaking course.

articles.title: In 2017, Stranger Things star Gaten Matarazzo helped form a charity for a disorder affecting roughly one in a million people; nine years later, its partners published 37 recommendations to guide medical care
articles.summary: When a medical condition affects only a tiny fraction of the population, even experienced doctors may struggle to find enough information to treat it.
articles.body: When a medical condition affects only a tiny fraction of the population, even experienced doctors may struggle to find enough information to treat it. This has been a longstanding challenge for people with cleidocranial dysplasia (CCD), a rare genetic disorder that affects the development of bones and teeth. Stranger Things actor Gaten Matarazzo, who was born with the condition, has used his public platform to raise awareness and support people facing similar challenges.A new study published online in the Journal of Bone and Mineral Research on January 8, 2026, marks an important development in that effort. Titled Diagnosis, treatment, and management recommendations for cleidocranial dysplasia: A modified Delphi panel, the research establishes 37 expert-consensus recommendations covering diagnosis, treatment and long-term medical care. The work involved specialists working with CCD Smiles, the nonprofit organisation Matarazzo and his family helped bring into formal operation in 2017, and researchers from Johns Hopkins and other institutions.How Matarazzo helped establish CCD SmilesMatarazzo, best known for playing Dustin Henderson in Netflix's Stranger Things, was born with cleidocranial dysplasia. The genetic condition affects skeletal development and can cause short or missing collarbones, delayed closure of the soft spots in the skull, and dental complications such as extra teeth and delayed eruption of permanent teeth. The disorder is estimated to affect approximately one in a million people worldwide. Its rarity has made it difficult for patients and families to find doctors with sufficient experience in managing its different complications.CCD Smiles was founded by Kelly Wosnik, a nurse practitioner who also lives with the condition. According to the organisation's account, Wosnik had been working towards establishing the foundation since 2013. Matarazzo's father contacted her in 2016, and together they helped make CCD Smiles an officially recognised nonprofit organisation in January 2017.The organisation focuses on raising awareness, supporting access to dental treatment and encouraging research. In a November 2025 interview with Cero Magazine, Matarazzo explained that patients often had to depend on doctors who had treated only a handful of people with the condition. He said he wanted medical professionals to have a reliable care plan explaining how to treat patients without taking steps that could cause harm or setbacks.Researchers developed 37 medical recommendationsTo address the lack of standardised guidance, a multidisciplinary panel of 13 experts conducted a three-round modified Delphi study. This method involves collecting expert opinions through repeated surveys and discussions until sufficient agreement is reached. The research produced 37 recommendations covering three broad areas: diagnosis, treatment and management, and the healthcare professionals involved in patient care.Of these, nine recommendations focused on diagnosis, while 24 covered treatment and management. The latter included seven dental and orthodontic recommendations and 17 other medical recommendations. The remaining four addressed care providers. The researchers described the findings as the first comprehensive best-practice recommendations to help patients, families and healthcare professionals understand and manage the condition.Guidance covers teeth, bones and overall healthA significant part of the recommendations addresses dental and orthodontic complications. Children with CCD should undergo orthodontic screening by a specialist experienced in the condition by the age of six. The panel also recommended regular dental monitoring through X-rays because some abnormalities may not be visible during ordinary oral examinations.Another important recommendation is that orthodontic treatment should be planned according to a patient's dental development rather than simply their chronological age. Specialists also recommended a phased approach to exposing unerupted teeth. Prosthetic options, including implants, bridges or dentures, may be considered for patients who cannot undergo or do not wish to pursue conventional orthodontic treatment.However, the recommendations extend beyond dental care. The panel highlighted the importance of hearing assessments, particularly after diagnosis, with annual testing until consistently normal results are recorded. Patients may also need regular orthopaedic evaluations, mobility assessments and monitoring of bone density because the condition can be associated with fractures and reduced bone strength.The experts further recommended access to counselling, mental health support and pain management when needed. They emphasised that people with CCD should continue receiving ordinary healthcare alongside specialised treatment.Coordinated care is a key recommendationThe study also stresses that managing CCD requires cooperation between different medical specialists. Depending on a patient's symptoms, their care team may include primary care doctors, dentists, orthodontists, geneticists, orthopaedic specialists, hearing specialists, endocrinologists and physical or occupational therapists. The recommendations are intended to help doctors recognise the condition earlier, understand its complications and coordinate treatment rather than approaching each problem separately.For Matarazzo and CCD Smiles, the research addresses a major gap that has affected people living with the disorder for years. While the recommendations do not offer a cure, they provide a shared medical reference for patients and professionals who previously had limited standardised guidance. The study also represents a significant step towards making care more consistent for people with a condition that remains unfamiliar to many healthcare providers.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2023, Jackass star Steve-O bought a 44-acre property outside Nashville; three years later, the ranch houses rescued goats, pigs, cats and dogs as he looks to expand its animal welfare mission
articles.summary: In 2023, Jackass star Steve-O bought a 44-acre property outside Nashville with an unusual ambition: to turn it into a sanctuary where rescued animals
articles.body: In 2023, Jackass star Steve-O bought a 44-acre property outside Nashville with an unusual ambition: to turn it into a sanctuary where rescued animals could live safely and be understood as individuals. Three years later, The Radical Ranch is home to goats, pigs, cats and dogs, while its founder is looking to expand the operation and welcome more animals in need. The ranch, located in rural Sumner County about an hour northeast of downtown Nashville, was founded by Stephen Glover, better known as Steve-O, and Lux Wright in 2023. It became a registered 501(c)(3) nonprofit in 2024, with a mission to care for animals in need while encouraging compassion through positive, personal encounters rather than shame or shock, as per report by Nashville Scene and details on The Radical Ranch's website. Read more about Steve-O's Radical Ranch here:From Hollywood to TennesseeSteve-O found the property while visiting Nashville for a UFC event at Bridgestone Arena in the summer of 2023. He had been searching for a suitable site in Colorado and Southern California, but said the Nashville-area property stood out immediately because of its wooded trails, space and potential for animal rescue.The land offered more acreage than he had originally planned to buy, but Steve-O told the Nashville Scene that it felt like the right fit. A one-mile looping trail around the property helped convince him that the site had the space and setting needed to build a sanctuary.The move also reflected practical concerns. Steve-O said he had been living in the Hollywood Hills when he began hearing that some homeowners were struggling to renew insurance because of wildfire risk, making a move away from California increasingly appealing.A sanctuary takes shapeThe Radical Ranch is now home to nine animals, including rescued goats, pigs, cats and dogs. Among them are three goats named Sam, Drake and Phil, who were acquired in 2019 while Steve-O was still living in the Hollywood Hills and became what he calls the sanctuary’s “starter kit.” The ranch also cares for Fonzarelli, a bristly-haired pig rescued after the owner of the animals became terminally ill and could no longer look after them. Steve-O said Fonzarelli arrived the day before the owner died, giving the pig a safe home at a moment when there were few alternatives, as per Parade Pets.Other residents include a cat named Winifred Winfrey and several rescued dogs. The animals are cared for full time by ranch hand Daniel Amaya, the nonprofit’s only employee, whom the organisation credits with providing daily feeding, care and attention.A mission built on compassionSteve-O’s interest in animal welfare began long before he bought the Tennessee property. He has said that his time in clown college and later work with circuses exposed him to the treatment of animals, leaving him increasingly uncomfortable with what he saw.That discomfort eventually became public advocacy. After speaking about circus animals during a 2006 television appearance, Steve-O was invited by PETA to take part in campaigns opposing the use of animals in circuses, and he later adopted a vegan lifestyle during his recovery.The Radical Ranch takes a different approach from much animal-rights campaigning. Rather than relying on distressing images or confrontational messaging, Steve-O wants visitors and supporters to encounter animals directly and recognise their intelligence, emotions and capacity for connection.Plans to growThe sanctuary’s next priority is expansion. Steve-O has said he would like to add cows, build additional fencing and eventually bring donkeys to the property, which he believes could also help protect cattle. He has also discussed converting a children’s playhouse into a chicken coop and creating a tunnel that would allow chickens to enter the goat pen and help control ticks. Horses remain a longer-term possibility, although Steve-O described them as requiring far more skill, work and resources, as per the reports.The ranch’s growth depends not only on land and animals but on funding, infrastructure and administration. Steve-O has acknowledged that establishing the nonprofit involved considerable paperwork, but the organisation says all donations go toward animal care, future rescues and paying its ranch hand.Opening the gatesFor now, The Radical Ranch is not open to the public because Steve-O also lives there. He has said he can imagine a future in which visitors are welcomed, but he is not ready to make that change while the property remains his home.Public visits could eventually help fundraising and allow more people to meet the animals, something Steve-O sees as central to the sanctuary’s purpose. Until then, the ranch shares photos, personalities and stories of its residents online, giving supporters a way to connect with the animals from afar.Supporters can also contribute through donations or through Steve-O’s tattoo fundraising offer. He said he began giving tattoos in exchange for charitable donations after people asked him for ink, with no fixed price, so that cost would not become a barrier to participation.A different kind of legacySteve-O built his reputation on fearlessness, chaos and outrageous stunts, but The Radical Ranch reveals another side of his public life. The same energy that once fuelled Jackass is now being directed toward fencing, animal care, fundraising and plans for future rescues.The sanctuary is still young, and its ambitions remain bigger than its current population of nine animals. Yet its foundation is already clear: a place where animals rescued from difficult circumstances can be cared for, respected and seen as more than background characters in someone else’s story.For Steve-O, the ranch represents a chance to turn compassion into something practical. As The Radical Ranch grows, it may become less a celebrity side project and more a lasting refuge for animals that need one.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: SC: People tend to violate curbs with vengeance
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Acknowledging that the enormous amount of judicial time spent over the years to tackle pollution in Delhi had yielded only marginal benefits,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Acknowledging that the enormous amount of judicial time spent over the years to tackle pollution in Delhi had yielded only marginal benefits, Supreme Court Friday said when more and more restrictions, without scientific basis, were put in place, people tended to violate them with a vengeance, reports Dhananjay Mahapatra.Reflecting on numerous orders and subsequent monitoring of their implementation to improve air quality, a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said, "To think we can achieve air quality of less than 100 (AQI) in Delhi during winters is utopian when 'very poor' and 'severe' have become the new normal."When amicus curiae and senior advocate Aparajita Singh flagged news reports on normal crackers being sold as green crackers and attributed part of the rising pollution to it, the ben-ch said the capital was witnessing bumper-to-bumper traf-fic for the last few days and wi-th so many cars remaining on the road for so many extra hours, it must be adding to the pollution load.Additional solicitor general Aishwarya Bhati attributed the traffic congestion to the festive season and senior advocate Sanjiv Sen, who was appearing for MCD, said the culture of distribution of gifts was one of the major reasons for the huge spurt in road traffic.At this juncture, Singh drew the court's attention to sale of normal crackers as green crackers in flagrant violation of court orders and warned of a huge post-Diwali spike in pollution levels. The bench said, "Diwali celebrations must be accompanied with public awareness campaigns. It is awareness that alone can curb pollution. No number of restrictions is going to work. More the number of orders from the court, the more the violations. That is the tendency of people. We will go by expert advice."The CJI said local councillors must create awareness among people. The bench said it would pass some orders and seek compliance from NCR states.Bhati informed the court that the Commission on Air Quality Management (CAQM), the expert body tasked with devising and implementing short-term, intermediate and long-term measures to tackle air pollution, had put Grad-ed Response Action Plan (GRAP) in place."Each stage of GRAP triggers more restrictions - stoppage of construction, bar on entry of BS-IV emission standard vehicles, sprinkling of water, staggered office hours," she said, adding that there was a massive augmentation of clean fuel public transport. "But every human activity contributes to pollution," Bhati added, pointing out that factories in Delhi operated on clean fuel and thermal power plants had been closed.She said the main polluti-on load came from vehicles as Delhi had a staggering numb-er of them. "Major contribu-tor to pollution in Delhi is vehicles and other local sources. Stubble burning in winters, which has drastically declined in Haryana and to some extent in Punjab, tips the scales because of the unique geographical position of Delhi and the wind direction make the national capital a receptor of pollution," the ASG said.Singh said monitoring implementation of anti-pollution measures was crucial and complained that transport vehicles continued to idle at MCD toll plazas at 126 entry points. Refuting the claim, Sen said after the integration of technology, no transport vehicle idled at any of the nine toll plazas, which handle 90% of commercial traffic into Delhi.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Dallas star Victoria Principal stepped away from Hollywood and now spends her time caring for rescued animals on a ranch; at 76, she has shared the recovery of a miniature horse named Halo with fans
articles.summary: Victoria Principal, best known as Pamela Barnes Ewing on the long-running television series Dallas, has built a very different life away from Hollywood,
articles.body: Victoria Principal, best known as Pamela Barnes Ewing on the long-running television series Dallas, has built a very different life away from Hollywood, one centred on rescued animals and the quiet rhythms of ranch life. At 76, the actor has been sharing updates about Halo, a miniature horse recovering in her care, offering fans a glimpse into the compassion that now shapes her days. Principal recently posted a tender photograph with the white mini-horse on social media, writing that she was “loving on Halo” as the animal recovered. The post, shared with her followers and reported by Parade, highlighted the personal side of an actor who has largely stepped back from the entertainment industry and dedicated herself to animal welfare.Life after DallasPrincipal became a household name through Dallas, portraying Pamela Barnes Ewing for nine years alongside Larry Hagman and Linda Gray. The role made her one of television’s most recognisable faces during the show’s peak years and established her as a defining figure of the era’s primetime drama.Since leaving the series, Principal has chosen a life that looks markedly different from the glamour associated with her television career. Rather than pursuing a constant presence in Hollywood, she has focused on her ranch, her animals and the slower, more hands-on work of caring for creatures that need help.Her social media posts suggest that this transition has been less a retreat than a redirection. The same warmth that once made Pamela Ewing a compelling television character now appears in the way Principal speaks about the animals in her care.Halo’s recoveryHalo is the latest animal to appear in Principal’s updates, and the miniature horse has clearly become part of the ranch family. In the photograph shared by Principal, she is seen cuddling the small white horse, with a caption that emphasised love, patience and recovery.The post gave fans a rare look at the practical reality of animal rescue. Recovery is not always dramatic or immediate; it often involves quiet days, close attention and the kind of steady care that Principal appears to provide at her ranch.For Principal, Halo is not simply a rescued animal but a companion with a story. The affectionate caption and photograph convey a relationship built on trust, something especially meaningful for an animal that has faced hardship.A ranch full of rescuesHalo is not the only animal Principal has introduced to her followers. Last autumn, she shared an image of Tommy, a rescue pony she described as her “first pony” and “my boy,” writing that they hugged as their hearts beat together.Tommy, a Shetland pony, appears to hold a special place in Principal’s life. Her post described him as an “old soul,” language that reflects the emotional depth she brings to her relationships with the animals around her.These updates reveal a ranch that is less a private estate and more a working sanctuary for animals in need. Principal’s posts regularly show her close to the creatures she cares for, whether she is holding a pony, sitting beside a horse or celebrating with friends at home.A birthday among animalsIn January, Principal marked her 76th birthday at the ranch with friends, cake and several of her beloved animals. She described the celebration as “perfect,” pairing the message with a photo of herself alongside one of her horses.The setting says much about the life she has chosen. Rather than marking the occasion with a public event or industry gathering, Principal spent it in the company of the animals and people closest to her.Her appearance in the birthday post also drew attention from fans, many of whom remarked on how little she seems to have changed since her Dallas years. Still, the more meaningful part of the image may be the setting itself, a ranch where rescued animals are treated as family.A lasting commitmentPrincipal’s animal advocacy has become one of the most consistent parts of her public life since stepping away from acting. Her posts do not present rescue work as a passing interest but as a daily commitment that shapes how she spends her time.The care she gives Halo and Tommy reflects a broader philosophy of giving animals a second chance. Whether an animal needs rehabilitation, companionship or simply a safe place to live, Principal’s ranch appears to offer all three.For fans who remember her as Pamela Ewing, these glimpses into her current life offer a different kind of connection. Victoria Principal may have left the spotlight, but she has found a purpose that is visible in every photograph, every recovery update and every animal she welcomes home.You use AI every day. articles.title: Cate Blanchett wins approval for a luxury garden at her Cornwall eco-home after neighbours raised concerns; locals had earlier accused the actor of encroaching on environmentally important land
articles.summary: Oscar-winning actor Cate Blanchett has secured approval for landscaping and outdoor features at her £1.6 million Cornwall property, following months of
articles.body: Oscar-winning actor Cate Blanchett has secured approval for landscaping and outdoor features at her £1.6 million Cornwall property, following months of scrutiny over plans for her coastal eco-home. The approved proposals include a grass driveway, hardwood decking, Cornish granite steps, trees, ornamental plants and boulders around the five-bedroom property in Mawgan Porth. The application also faced questions over outdoor lighting, with ecological experts warning that some proposed fixtures could disturb bats foraging in the surrounding area. The revised lighting arrangements were subsequently accepted by Cornwall Council. The development has attracted criticism from some neighbours over the years, particularly over construction disruption and a separate proposal involving an adjoining meadow.Cate Blanchett's luxury garden plans at Cornwall eco-home get council approvalBlanchett and her husband, Australian playwright Andrew Upton, have received approval for details relating to landscaping, outdoor lighting and shutters at their property, known as Bob Tails, in Mawgan Porth, near Newquay.The approved plans include the addition of local plants, trees and ornamental grasses, along with Cornish boulders to complement the coastal surroundings. The proposals also feature a grass driveway, hardwood decking beside the house and steps made using Cornish granite.The decision was issued on July 14, 2026, under planning application PA26/03634. It concerns the discharge of three conditions attached to the original planning permission granted in September 2022, rather than a completely new permission to construct the house.Bat concerns prompted changes to the outdoor lightingOne of the main issues during the planning process involved the potential impact of outdoor lighting on bats in the area.The original landscaping proposals included several types of lighting, including pole-mounted path lights, tree-mounted spike lights, low-level step lights and wall lights. An ecological assessment raised concerns that some of the proposed fixtures did not comply with the bat-protection guidance referenced in the property's original planning conditions.A survey conducted in 2021 found no active bat roosts in the building. However, it established that bats used the wider site for foraging, prompting recommendations to minimise artificial lighting.The guidance called for low-level lights directed downwards, warm-spectrum illumination and timers to limit unnecessary use. Following the concerns, the couple submitted revised plans in May 2026.The amended arrangements use warm-white LED lighting in line with guidance from the Bat Conservation Trust. A representative for the couple told the Daily Mail that changes had been made to make the lighting more suitable for bats.How the Cornwall eco-home became a source of controversyBlanchett and Upton purchased a cottage in Mawgan Porth for approximately £1.6 million in 2020. The couple subsequently secured planning permission to demolish the existing property and replace it with a five-bedroom sustainable home.The construction project attracted complaints from some residents, who raised concerns about the scale of the development, building activity and its impact on the coastal village.In February 2024, The Guardian reported complaints from Karen Burgess, who owned a nearby holiday rental. She claimed that noise from construction work had disrupted guests' stays during 2023 and cost her business more than £60,000 in lost revenue.The couple's architects, Watershedd, disputed the allegations, saying that the noise described by Burgess must have originated from other developments in the area. The firm also said it had maintained communication with neighbours during the construction process.Neighbours objected to plans involving an adjoining meadowThe controversy extended beyond the construction of the house when Blanchett and Upton sought to develop an adjoining plot of land they had purchased in 2021.The couple proposed creating a new entrance and parking area for four cars on part of the land. The plans prompted objections from local residents concerned about the potential loss of green space and changes to the character of the surrounding landscape.One neighbour, Helen John, described the proposal as "a blatant attempt to erode an environmentally important piece of land by stealth and incorporate it".The couple's planning representatives, Situ8, defended the proposal, arguing that the loss of green space would be limited and that approximately 86% of the meadow would remain. They also maintained that the proposed parking area had been designed to minimise its visual impact.The separate application was eventually withdrawn in June 2024. A letter informing Cornwall Council of the withdrawal did not publicly specify the reason for the decision.The property that earned Mawgan Porth the 'Hollywood-on-Sea' nicknameMawgan Porth is a coastal village near Newquay in Cornwall that has attracted several well-known figures in recent years. Its association with celebrity homeowners has led to the nickname "Hollywood-on-Sea".Actors including Stanley Tucci, Jason Statham and Jason Momoa have also been linked to the area in media reports.Blanchett's property has drawn particular attention because of its coastal location and the controversy surrounding its redevelopment. The couple's project was presented as a sustainable replacement for the original cottage, incorporating a modern five-bedroom home within the coastal landscape.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Texas beverage company borrowed $2 million in 2021 and its co-owner signed a limited $500,000 personal guaranty. After a default, an appeals court upheld a $619,419.50 judgment including interest on Oct. 30
articles.summary: A business loan can put more than just the company’s finances at risk.
articles.body: A business loan can put more than just the company’s finances at risk. If a lender asks an owner to personally guaranty some of the borrowing, the consequences can haunt them long after the business runs into trouble. That was the case in a dispute involving Texas beverage maker Holy Kombucha, after a lender came after one of its co-owners over a guaranty signed as part of a loan restructuring.On Oct. 30, 2026, the Texas Sixth Court of Appeals upheld a judgment against Theresa Pham for $619,419.50 to Montgomery Capital Partners IV, LP. The award was $500,000 in damages and $119,419.50 in pre-judgment interest. The decision upheld the trial court’s finding that Pham’s guaranty was still in place when the company defaulted.How the guaranty was triggeredAccording to the Texas Sixth Court of Appeals, Montgomery Capital Partners loaned $2 million to Holy Kombucha, Inc., partially owned by Pham and Leandro Bienati, in January 2021. After a first default, the company entered into a forbearance agreement in December of that year.Under the agreement the lender agreed to provide the business with a $500,000 draw facility. As part of the agreement, Pham was required to sign a personal guaranty. At the time of the loan, the original loan balance was $2,044,544.92.Pham’s liability was limited by the guaranty to the lesser of $500,000 or the total principal advances made under the new draw facility. It also provided that her obligation would terminate when the aggregate of the principal and interest outstanding on the original loan and draw facility fell to or below the stated balance.The company burned cash and defaulted again in April 2024. Montgomery then sued Pham for breach of the guaranty.Dispute over whether the obligation was extinguishedOne key question was whether Pham’s personal guaranty had already been extinguished. She argued the draw facility was paid off in April 2022 and the conditions to terminate her obligation were therefore met.The Texas Sixth Court of Appeals looked at the payment history and correspondence that was offered at trial. Holy Kombucha had paid down a substantial amount on the draw facility, but the lender claimed there remained some interest owed. It also held that the guaranty covered the net balance of the original term loan and the draw facility and not just the draw facility.The lender prevailed at the trial court. The results showed that the total guarantyd debt never fell below the threshold of $2,044,544.92. The appeals court found the evidence was sufficient to support that finding and rejected Pham’s argument that the warranty had expired.Why the decision was upheldPham also took issue with where the lawsuit was filed, the admission of a loan balance sheet and how interest was calculated. But the Texas Sixth Court of Appeals said those arguments offered no reason to overturn the judgment.As to venue, the court said Pham had not made a timely request for a hearing on her motion to move the case to Dallas County. Her objection to the venue was therefore waived. The guaranty also provided the lender the right to initiate proceedings in other jurisdictions, including the court where it filed the case.The court also admitted in evidence a balance sheet showing the advances on the loan, repayments and interest accrued. It said the lender’s representative had provided adequate proof of how the records were kept. Pham’s separate objections to disclosure rules had not been properly raised at trial.She also challenged the award of interest, but that was rejected because she did not make that argument in the trial court. The judgment awarded pre-judgment interest at a contractual rate of 16 per cent compounded daily.There was a dissent though. Justice Jeff Rambin disagreed with the majority opinion on the balance sheet, arguing that the document was created for litigation purposes shortly before the trial and therefore should not have been admitted as a routine business record.The majority disagreed but affirmed the trial court's judgment and the award of $619,419.50 against Pham.You use AI every day. articles.title: Creamy layer verdict only for those who challenged government decision, says SC
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Friday said its March 2026 verdict quashing Centre's 2004 decision to factor in salary income of PSU and private sector employees
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Friday said its March 2026 verdict quashing Centre's 2004 decision to factor in salary income of PSU and private sector employees for deciding creamy layer status for OBCs would be applicable only to those who had moved the court, while those already appointed and allotted cadre would not be disturbed.The clarification came following apprehension in many quarters that the March order would affect all subsequent appointments as those denied reservation in the last decades on that calculation would become eligible for fresh entry into the civil services.In March, SC had held that income of parents could not be the sole criterion to determine whether a candidate fell in the creamy layer for exclusion from OBC reservation and the status and category of parents' job had to be considered along with 'income/wealth test' as an additional criterion of exclusion.Order won't be ground to reopen appointments already made: SCThe ruling has huge implications for wards of PSU and private sector employees as in their case, parents' income was taken as the sole factor to determine creamy layer status, unlike in the case of govt job employees whose category of job was the deciding factor. As it created uncertainty over the validity of the recruitment process for OBC candidates over the years, Centre sought clarification from Supreme Court, saying its order should not be enforced retrospectively.The bench said, "The judgement determines the rights of the parties before this court. It holds that the respondent candidates fall within the non-creamy layer of the OBC category and are entitled to the benefit of reservation together with consequential placement and allotment of posts in the selection processes in which they participated. The grant of such benefit shall not, by itself, operate to the detriment of the seniority of any other person or entail the reopening of selections or appointments already concluded."Advocates Shashank Ratnoo and Varun Thakur, who represented the candidates who have been fighting a legal battle for years, said govt has to create supernumerary posts to accommodate their clients who fulfil the requisite eligibility conditions.The Supreme Court said its judgement shall not, by itself, furnish a ground for reopening selections or appointments already concluded prior to the order and the claims of those asserting that they are similarly placed and whose cases are pending before any court, tribunal or other competent forum or authority, may be considered on their own merits."This court expresses no opinion on the merits of such claims, save to reiterate that the interpretation of the 1993 OM and the 2004 letter laid down in the judgement may be taken into consideration while adjudicating such claims in accordance with law," the bench said.The office memorandum (OM) issued by Centre in 1993 had said the same principle would be applied to employees of PSUs, banks, insurance organisations, universities and similar bodies holding equivalent or comparable posts. But the "equivalence of posts" as contemplated in the OM was not done and a clarificatory letter was issued by govt in 2004 making 'income/wealth test' the sole criterion for PSUs and private sector employees.The court, however, had said overemphasis on the 2004 letter to the extent of making income alone determinative without regard to parental status or category of service would defeat the structural framework of exclusion envisaged under the 1993 office memorandum and there could not be different criteria for children of govt employees and the rest.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Stephen Miller: Key architect of Trump's immigration crackdown appointed White House chief of staff
articles.summary: Stephen Miller, one of US President Donald Trump's longest-serving advisers and the architect of his hardline immigration agenda, has been named the new
articles.body: Stephen Miller, one of US President Donald Trump's longest-serving advisers and the architect of his hardline immigration agenda, has been named the new White House chief of staff, placing a key figure behind the administration's domestic policies at the centre of its decision-making.The 41-year-old will replace Susie Wiles, becoming Trump's closest aide at a time when Republicans have suffered a setback in the midterm elections and Democrats are set to take control of Congress. Wiles became the first woman to hold the position during Trump's second presidency.Meanwhile, Miller's appointment also puts an official closely involved in some of the administration's most controversial decisions in a position to coordinate its response to the incoming opposition.A central figure in Trump's immigration agendaMiller's association with Trump dates back to the 2016 presidential campaign. He joined the campaign as a speechwriter and subsequently became a senior adviser in Trump's first administration, serving from 2017 to 2021. His influence continued after Trump returned to the White House in 2025, when Miller took charge of policy coordination as deputy chief of staff and also served as homeland security adviser.Immigration has been his most prominent area of involvement. Miller has long argued for stricter controls and played a central role in turning Trump's campaign promises on immigration into government policy.During the second administration, he pushed for a daily target of 3,000 arrests by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The enforcement drive expanded operations across American communities, bringing people without criminal convictions within the scope of immigration raids. Even long-term residents were caught up in the crackdown.Miller also encouraged ICE to conduct operations at Home Depot outlets, where day labourers frequently gather. His position has extended to changing the legal framework governing immigration. He has repeatedly backed an end to birthright citizenship, which guarantees citizenship to most people born on US soil.After the Supreme Court rejected Trump's proposal on birthright citizenship, Miller described the decision as "one of the most destructive and outrageous decisions" in the court's history, as quoted by Reuters. He subsequently announced a move against so-called birth tourism, targeting foreign nationals travelling to the US to have children.The immigration crackdown has, however, become a source of political opposition for the administration. A Reuters/Ipsos survey conducted shortly before the midterm elections found that 54% of respondents disapproved of the enforcement drive, against 36% who approved of it. Democrats have indicated that Miller's role in the policy will come under congressional scrutiny.Beyond immigrationMiller has also been involved in several other major initiatives pursued by Trump. These include the administration's efforts to reduce the federal workforce, which resulted in tens of thousands of civil servants losing their jobs in 2025, and its disputes with universities and institutions over diversity programmes.He has been an advocate of expanding presidential authority and is part of a small group of White House officials involved in reviewing executive orders.His political positions also extend to foreign policy. Miller has defended US military operations against suspected drug-smuggling vessels in the Caribbean and Pacific and supported American and Israeli military action against Iran. He has also backed the administration's pressure on Tehran through sanctions and a naval blockade.In January, he refused to rule out military action as a means of acquiring Greenland. Defending the administration's attacks on suspected drug smugglers in October 2025, he said: "These are terrorists and they're going to be killed."How Miller entered Trump's political orbitMiller's political views took shape long before he joined Trump's campaign. Raised in Santa Monica, California, he developed a reputation for conservative and combative commentary while writing for Duke University's student newspaper.He subsequently worked as a congressional aide, where he advocated restricting immigration at a time when the position had not yet become a defining feature of Republican politics. His association with Trump gave him a national platform and an opportunity to translate those views into policy.Following Trump's defeat in the 2020 election, Miller established America First Legal, a conservative advocacy organisation. The group pursued complaints against companies, including Nike, alleging discrimination against white people.Miller has remained a close political ally of Trump throughout the president's two terms. His wife, Katie Miller, is a conservative podcaster who previously worked as a communications aide in Trump's first administration.What his elevation means for TrumpMiller's appointment comes at a time when Trump faces the prospect of congressional investigations into his administration and its policies. Democrats have already signalled that the new chief of staff could be among their targets.Hakeem Jeffries, who is set to become the Democratic speaker of the House, described Miller as a "reckless extremist" after the announcement. Representative Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee, also warned that Miller should prepare for scrutiny over the administration's immigration operations.Marc Short, who served as chief of staff to former Vice-President Mike Pence, said Miller's elevation showed that Trump wanted an adviser firmly aligned with him and prepared to confront lawmakers. As per him, Trump was "getting someone who is wed to him" and willing to battle Congress over immigration and investigations.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: BENGALURU: Karnataka govt-authorised lab tests of E20 blend have found “excess” mixing of ethanol by more than 10% per litre of petrol in several samples.
articles.body: BENGALURU: Karnataka govt-authorised lab tests of E20 blend have found “excess” mixing of ethanol by more than 10% per litre of petrol in several samples.On Friday, state food and civil supplies and legal metrology minister Rizwan Arshad shared the results for samples collected from 63 petrol bunks across Karnataka.The samples included fuel from IOCL, HPCL, BPCL, Nayara, Shell and MRPL facilities. Tests of samples from 14 of the bunks found ethanol levels above the prescribed limit.The results revealed ethanol blending of 31.2% and 30.5% at some IOCL and HPCL petrol bunks, respectively, which were way beyond the stipulated 20%. Blending at some BPCL, Nayara, and Shell bunks was also found to be beyond the prescribed limit.The minister claimed that an estimated 10% drop in mileage due to ethanol blending would cost consumers as much as Rs 62,000 crore, based on petrol sales of 6,200 crore litres between April 2025 and April 2026 at Rs 100-110 per litre.Arshad said under the directives of chief minister DK Shivakumar, his department conducted the inspections across Karnataka. “The results have raised serious concerns over transparency, regulatory compliance, and consumers’ right to know what goes in the fuel [they’re using],” Arshad added.He further clarified that neither he nor Karnataka govt was against blending of ethanol in petrol. “However, I am against the handling of the entire issue by central govt and the way people are being penalised,” he added.In its recommendation, Karnataka govt demanded that the Centre publicly clarify the “actual ethanol blend” being supplied to consumers, and penalties be imposed on all OMCs supplying petrol above 20% ethanol blend. It has also pressed for E20 spoilage fund to compensate every consumer for the loss incurred.The state govt has sought mandatory blend displays at fuel pumps across the nation to allow consumers to choose between the range of blends available.OMCs question sampling and testing methodsIOCL, BPCL and HPCL said Friday E20 petrol supplied by them across India, including in Karnataka, conforms to the Bureau of Indian Standards specification. The three public sector Oil Marketing Companies also raised concerns about the sampling procedure and methodology adopted for the tests.They said the Oct samples were collected without OMC representatives and that the companies had not received outlet-wise reports, retention samples or details needed to verify the results. articles.body: BENGALURU: In a series of grisly murders committed over a 15-day period in late Oct, a 52-year-old cab driver allegedly killed his wife and six members of her extended family and dumped their bodies at four locations in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. His wife, mother-in-law and seven-year-old nephew were among the victims, police said.Police identified the accused as S Indushekhar alias Arjun Indushekhar, who lived in Rajajinagar’s V Block. When he was arrested near Ulsoorgate on Wednesday, a minor boy — said to be his eighth target — was found in his car. “Indushekhar claimed he had planned to kill the boy as well,” a police officer said, adding the accused is being interrogated in police custody.His daughter, 17, is suspected to have helped him in committing multiple murders.Police alleged the accused invited the victims to his second-floor house between Oct 16 and 31 for lunch or dinner, and crushed them to death with a grindstone. During questioning, Indushekhar allegedly told investigators he had been ‘in conflict with’ his wife for nearly 20 years and blamed the relatives for supporting her during their disputes.The victims were identified as his wife Sunita (40); mother-in-law Rupavathi (65); brother-in-law Shivakumar (46); his wife Divya (30); brother-in-law Shankar (44); his wife Nalini (29); and their son Puneeth (7). Police commissioner Seemant Kumar Singh called the incident “serious” and added that the motive appears to be personal. The case came to light after relatives of the missing persons failed to establish contact with them and sought help from police to find their whereabouts.Thunganamma approached Srirampura police on Nov 3 to report that her daughter Nalini, Shankar and several relatives were missing, and their phones remained switched off on Oct 31 and Nov 1.Kalavathi similarly separately reported to police about her daughter Divya, son-in-law Shivakumar and grandson Puneeth.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bengaluru | Silver Rate in Bengaluru | Bank Holidays in Bengaluru | Public Holidays in Bengaluru | Bengaluru AQI | Weather in Bengaluru | Petrol Price in Bengaluru | Diesel Price in Bengaluru | CNG Price in Bengaluru | LPG Price in BengaluruStay updated with the latest Bengaluru news.
